question: Where to hire fractional Chief Revenue Officers?
body:
## Direct Answer
You can hire a fractional Chief Revenue Officer through specialized executive marketplaces (Bolster, Go Fractional, Chief Outsiders, Continuum), operator communities (Pavilion, RevGenius, RevOps Co-op), your own investor and advisor network, or vetted talent platforms like Toptal and Catalant. The right channel depends on your stage, budget, and how much vetting you want done for you before the first conversation.

Hiring a fractional CRO is less about finding a warm body with the title and more about matching a specific revenue problem — pipeline stalls, a broken sales motion, a founder-led sales handoff, a pricing reset — to an operator who has solved exactly that problem before. The channels below each optimize for a different tradeoff between speed, cost, vetting depth, and fit, and the best hire almost always comes from running two or three of them in parallel rather than betting on one. Think of the search as a portfolio: a marketplace gives you speed and legal scaffolding, a community gives you honest reputation signal, and your cap table gives you accountability, and the strongest shortlists borrow from all three at once.

## What is a fractional CRO and when do you actually need one?
A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a senior revenue leader who owns your go-to-market strategy — sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, and often customer success — on a part-time, fixed-scope, or interim basis instead of as a full-time salaried executive. They typically work anywhere from one to three days a week across one or several companies, and the engagement is structured as a monthly retainer or a defined project rather than an employment contract. The point is to buy the judgment of someone who has scaled revenue from, say, $2M to $20M before, without paying the full loaded cost of a permanent CRO while you are still proving the motion works.

You need one when the revenue problem is a leadership problem, not a headcount problem. The classic trigger is the founder-led-sales ceiling: the founder has personally closed the first fifty customers, but the motion lives entirely in their head, reps are missing quota because there is no repeatable playbook, and the founder cannot both sell and build the machine that lets others sell. Other clean triggers are a stalled Series A/B where the board wants a professional revenue operator before committing to a full-time hire, a post-acquisition integration that needs an interim steady hand, or a pricing-and-packaging reset that requires cross-functional authority. If your problem is simply "we need more reps," you need a sales manager and a recruiter, not a fractional CRO. For a deeper breakdown of the decision, see our guide at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-fractional-cro-vs-vp-sales.

![Where to hire fractional Chief Revenue Officers — figure 1](/assets/qa/tl9004-b1.jpg)


It is worth being honest about when a fractional CRO is the wrong tool, because hiring one at the wrong moment wastes money on both sides. If your product has not found problem-solution fit, no revenue leader can systematize a motion that does not yet exist — you are still in the founder's discovery phase, and the founder is irreplaceable there. If you already have a proven, repeatable motion and simply need someone to run the daily cadence, a full-time VP of Sales is a better and cheaper fit than a part-time executive who is dividing attention across clients. And if the real issue is that the founder does not want to sell anymore, a fractional CRO will not fix a motivation problem dressed up as a capability problem. The clean signal that you genuinely need one is this: you can see revenue that should exist, you have some early proof it is reachable, and the gap between here and there is systems, leadership, and judgment rather than raw effort or headcount.

```mermaid

  A[Revenue problem surfaces] --> B{Is it strategy or headcount}
  B -->|Strategy and system| C[Consider a fractional CRO]
  B -->|More reps needed| D[Hire sales manager and recruiter]
  C --> E{What is the trigger}
  E --> F[Founder led sales ceiling]
  E --> G[Board wants operator before full time]
  E --> H[Interim after departure or acquisition]
  E --> I[Pricing and motion reset]

  G --> J

```

## Where are the best marketplaces to hire a fractional CRO?
The fastest path for most funded startups is a marketplace built specifically for fractional and interim executives, because the vetting, contracting, and matching are already handled. **Bolster** is one of the most established — co-founded by former Return Path CEO Matt Blumberg, it maintains a large vetted network of fractional CxOs and is often used by VC-backed companies because it plugs directly into investor referral flows. **Go Fractional** focuses squarely on the fractional model and curates operators by function, making it easy to browse revenue leaders specifically. **Continuum** (formerly Catalant's exec arm and now its own platform) and **Catalant** itself lean toward more established, mid-market and enterprise engagements where the CRO may run a defined transformation project.

For services-heavy or hands-on operating help, **Chief Outsiders** is a well-known firm that places fractional CMOs and CROs as part of a bench with shared methodology and support — you are hiring a firm's operator rather than an independent, which trades some cost and flexibility for continuity and backup. On the broader talent side, **Toptal** has an executive and finance/ops network that increasingly includes go-to-market leaders, and it is useful when you want platform-managed contracts and a fast replacement guarantee. The tradeoff across all marketplaces is the same: they compress your search from weeks to days and handle the awkward parts (rates, contracts, replacement if it doesn't work), but you pay a premium versus sourcing directly, and the "vetted" label still requires you to run your own reference and scenario checks. We cover how to evaluate a marketplace candidate at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-vet-fractional-exec.

![Where to hire fractional Chief Revenue Officers — figure 3](/assets/qa/tl9004-b3.jpg)


It helps to understand what a marketplace actually does and does not de-risk. What it de-risks well is logistics: a standardized statement of work, a rate that has been benchmarked against comparable engagements, a payments and compliance layer so you are not chasing invoices or worrying about worker-classification exposure, and — on the stronger platforms — a replacement guarantee if the first match does not click within the first few weeks. What it does not de-risk is fit for your specific motion. A marketplace's vetting confirms that a person is who they say they are and has held the roles they claim; it cannot confirm that a leader who scaled outbound enterprise sales will thrive fixing a product-led self-serve funnel. That judgment stays with you no matter how polished the platform is.

The practical move is to post or browse on two marketplaces at once and treat the first three intro calls as calibration — you are learning what a good fractional CRO for *your* stage sounds like before you commit to anyone. Rates on these platforms vary widely by seniority, scope, and geography, so anchor on scope of outcomes rather than a day rate in isolation. A useful discipline is to write a one-page brief before you ever open a marketplace profile: the specific revenue problem, the stage and current numbers, the motion (PLG, inbound, outbound, channel, enterprise), the decision you need the operator to unblock, and the outcome you would call success ninety days in. That brief does double duty — it filters the marketplace matches, and it becomes the spine of the eventual scope of work.

## Can you hire a fractional CRO through operator communities instead?
Yes, and for many early-stage founders the community channel produces better fit at lower cost than a marketplace, because you are sourcing from people who already live inside the RevOps and sales-leadership world. **Pavilion** (the community formerly known as Revenue Collective) is the flagship here — it is a membership organization of go-to-market executives, and its member directory, job board, and Slack channels are full of current and aspiring fractional CROs. Posting an interim or fractional need inside Pavilion reaches operators who are actively between full-time roles or deliberately building a portfolio of fractional clients. **RevGenius** and the **RevOps Co-op** (now part of the broader RevOps community landscape) serve similar functions with a stronger operations and systems bent, which matters if your revenue problem is as much about tooling and process as it is about selling.

The community route requires more work from you: there is no platform running background checks, standardizing contracts, or guaranteeing a replacement. You are trading convenience for signal. The upside is that community references are unusually honest — the RevOps and sales-leadership world is small and reputationally tight, so a quick back-channel through two mutual connections tells you more than any formal reference. LinkedIn is the connective tissue for all of this: search for people whose headline literally reads "Fractional CRO" or "Fractional Revenue Leader," look at whether they have a genuine multi-client portfolio (a real fractional operator, not a between-jobs executive using the label as a placeholder), and read how they talk about outcomes. For guidance on structuring the engagement once you find someone this way, see https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-fractional-cro-contract-scope.

There is a softer benefit to the community channel that is easy to underrate: you can watch a candidate operate before you ever talk to them. In a place like Pavilion or RevGenius, the strongest fractional leaders are visible in how they answer other members' questions — whether they reach for a framework or a war story, whether they think in systems or anecdotes, whether they are generous or self-promotional. That public track record is a truer sample of how someone thinks than a polished intro call, and it costs you nothing but reading time. The corresponding risk is selection bias: the most active community voices are not always the best operators, only the most available ones, so treat visibility as a lead, not a verdict, and still run the same structured evaluation you would run on any other source.

## How do you use your investor and advisor network to find one?
If you have raised institutional money, your cap table is a hiring channel you have already paid for, and it is frequently the highest-signal source of all. Venture and growth funds keep informal benches of operators they trust, because placing a strong fractional or interim CRO into a portfolio company protects their investment. Ask your lead investor directly: "Who is the best fractional revenue leader you've placed into a portfolio company at our stage?" A referral that comes with the investor's own track record attached carries built-in accountability — the operator knows their reputation with a fund that sends repeat business is on the line, which changes their incentives in your favor.

Board members, existing advisors, and other founders in your investor's portfolio are the next ring. Founders who have just come through the exact transition you are facing — founder-led sales to a repeatable motion — can hand you a name and a candid assessment in a single Slack message. The weakness of the network channel is coverage: it only works if your network happens to contain the right operator for your specific motion (PLG versus enterprise sales, for instance, are entirely different skill sets), and warm referrals can carry a bias toward "nice to work with" over "will actually hit the number." Counter that by treating a referred candidate to the same structured evaluation you would give a cold marketplace hire — reference the *outcomes*, not the relationship. Our framework for that structured evaluation lives at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-fractional-cro-90-day-plan.

Many funds now have a formal talent or platform team whose entire job is to make introductions like this, so do not assume the informal ask is your only option — send the request to your partner and to the talent lead in the same week, and be specific about stage, motion, and timing. Larger firms sometimes maintain executive-in-residence or operator-in-residence programs, and an EIR between company-building stints can be an unusually strong fractional match because the fund already vouches for them and they are hungry for a live problem. The one thing to watch is alignment of interest: an investor's job is to protect the round, which usually points the same direction as your success, but occasionally a fund pushes a favored operator to shore up a struggling portfolio relationship rather than because they are the best fit for you. You defend against that the same way you defend against a warm-referral halo everywhere else — by grounding the decision in the candidate's own before-and-after revenue outcomes rather than in who made the introduction.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Start search] --> B[Marketplaces]
  A --> C[Operator communities]
  A --> D[Investor and advisor network]
  A --> E[Talent platforms]
  B --> F[Shortlist of three to five]
  C --> F
  D --> F
  E --> F
  F --> G[Structured scenario interview]
  G --> H[Reference outcomes not relationships]
  H --> I[Paid trial or scoped first month]
  I --> J[Decision to extend or replace]
```

## What should you evaluate before signing, regardless of where you found them?
The channel gets you a shortlist; a disciplined evaluation gets you the right hire. Start with pattern-match on stage and motion. A fractional CRO who scaled a $50M enterprise sales org is often the wrong choice for a $3M product-led company, and vice versa — the reflexes that worked at one stage actively harm the other. Ask each candidate to walk through the single most similar situation to yours from their portfolio, in specifics: what the pipeline looked like, what they changed in the first thirty days, what the number did, and what they would do differently. Vague answers about "building high-performing teams" are a red flag; a strong operator talks in concrete before-and-after metrics.

Second, insist on a scoped first engagement rather than an open-ended retainer. The best fractional CROs will propose a diagnostic period — often the first thirty days — where they audit your funnel, sales data, comp plans, and pipeline hygiene and come back with a written plan and a set of committed outcomes. That deliverable is both the value and the audition. Third, get the operating model explicit in writing: days per week, who they manage versus advise, what authority they have over hiring and comp, how they report to you and the board, and — critically — the exit ramp to a full-time CRO, because a good fractional leader is often hiring their own eventual replacement. Finally, run real references on *revenue outcomes*, not personality: call a founder who worked with them and ask whether the number moved and whether they would rehire. Because the fractional model means your CRO has other clients, also confirm there is no competitive conflict and that your engagement has genuine priority. These evaluation mechanics matter more than which marketplace or community produced the name — the sourcing channel is a funnel, and the evaluation is the filter that actually determines whether the hire works.

A few practical mechanics tighten the filter further. Give the same short scenario to every finalist — a real, anonymized slice of your funnel or a live pricing dilemma — and compare how they reason, not just what they conclude; the shape of the thinking is what you are actually buying. Watch how they handle disagreement in the room, because a fractional CRO with real authority will need to tell you and your board things you do not want to hear, and one who only mirrors your assumptions is worthless at the moment it counts. Confirm the practical load-bearing details before the excitement of a good call carries you past them: how many other clients they hold, which days are genuinely yours, how fast they respond when a deal is on fire mid-week, and what happens to your engagement if one of their other clients suddenly demands more. And define the off-ramp as carefully as the on-ramp — a clean notice period, a knowledge-transfer expectation, and a rule that any playbook, CRM configuration, and documentation they build belongs to you, so the motion survives their departure. The whole point of hiring fractionally is to install a system that outlasts the person; an engagement that leaves no durable artifact behind has failed even if the number moved while they were there.

## Related questions
### How much does a fractional CRO cost?
Pricing is engagement-specific and varies by seniority, days per week, and scope, so anchor on outcomes rather than a headline day rate. Most arrangements are monthly retainers tied to a defined scope; always compare the fully loaded cost against the risk-adjusted cost of a wrong full-time hire.

### Fractional CRO vs. VP of Sales — which do I need?
A fractional CRO owns cross-functional revenue strategy (sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, CS) part-time; a VP of Sales owns and runs the sales team full-time. Hire the fractional CRO when the problem is strategy and system; hire the VP when you have a proven motion that just needs day-to-day leadership.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run six to eighteen months — long enough to install a repeatable motion and, often, to hire and onboard a permanent full-time CRO. Structure it with a 30-day diagnostic, then quarter-by-quarter renewals tied to committed outcomes rather than an open-ended retainer.

### Can a fractional CRO become full-time?
Sometimes, and it can be a low-risk trial-to-hire path, but many career fractional operators deliberately keep a portfolio of clients and prefer to hire their own full-time replacement. Clarify the intent early so expectations on both sides are aligned before you sign.

### Which channel is fastest to a signed engagement?
Marketplaces are usually fastest because vetting and contracts are pre-built — days to intro calls, two to three weeks to signed. Your investor network can match that speed when the right operator happens to be on the bench, while community sourcing is fastest for fit but slowest on the paperwork you have to handle yourself.

## FAQ
**What is the difference between a fractional CRO and an interim CRO?**
A fractional CRO works part-time on an ongoing basis, often across several clients simultaneously. An interim CRO is usually full-time but temporary — a bridge to cover a sudden departure or lead a specific transition until a permanent hire lands. Both are sourced through the same channels.

**How quickly can I hire a fractional CRO?**
Through a marketplace like Bolster or Go Fractional, you can be in intro calls within days and signed within two to three weeks. Community and network sourcing can be just as fast if the right operator is available, but the vetting and contracting fall on you.

**Should an early-stage startup hire a fractional CRO or a first sales rep?**
If you have no repeatable motion yet, a fractional CRO helps you build one and tells you what kind of reps to hire and when. If the motion already works and you simply need capacity, hire reps first — a CRO with no team to lead is premature.

**Do fractional CROs work with pre-revenue companies?**
Generally the fit is weak pre-revenue, because there is no motion to systematize and no data to diagnose. The value shows up once you have early customers and a founder-led sales ceiling. Pre-revenue, an advisor or fractional GTM strategist on a lighter engagement is usually a better spend.

**How do I know if a fractional CRO is legitimate versus just between jobs?**
Look for a genuine multi-client portfolio, a repeatable diagnostic-to-plan methodology, and references who confirm the revenue number moved. Someone using "Fractional CRO" as a placeholder while job-hunting will lack a real portfolio and will steer conversations toward full-time conversion.

**Can I hire a fractional CRO through Toptal or other talent platforms?**
Yes — platforms like Toptal and Catalant increasingly include senior go-to-market operators and handle contracting and replacement guarantees. They work best when you want platform-managed logistics and a fast backfill option, though you should still run your own outcome-focused references.

**What does a fractional CRO actually own day to day?**
Typically the revenue strategy and operating cadence: pipeline review, forecast accuracy, comp and quota design, sales-marketing alignment, RevOps tooling, and coaching frontline managers. What they directly manage versus advise should be written into the engagement so authority is unambiguous.

**How do I structure the first 30 days with a fractional CRO?**
Scope it as a diagnostic: they audit funnel data, comp plans, pipeline hygiene, and win/loss, then deliver a written plan with committed outcomes and a proposed operating model. That deliverable is both the value and the audition before you commit to a longer retainer.

**Should I hire an independent fractional CRO or one attached to a firm like Chief Outsiders?**
An independent gives you lower cost, more flexibility, and a direct relationship; a firm-backed operator gives you shared methodology, peer support, and a built-in backup if your leader is unavailable or the fit fails. Choose the firm when continuity and coverage matter more than cost and customization.

**How many clients is it acceptable for a fractional CRO to hold at once?**
There is no fixed number, but two to four is a common healthy range for genuine part-time engagements. What matters is that your allotted days are protected and their responsiveness during a live deal crisis is real — ask directly how they triage when two clients need them the same day.

**Who owns the playbooks and CRM setup my fractional CRO builds?**
You should — make it explicit in the contract that any documentation, CRM configuration, comp models, and playbooks created during the engagement are your property. The entire value of the model is a durable system that outlasts the person, so a clean IP and knowledge-transfer clause is non-negotiable.
